clue.text: Criminals will get sign of disapproval always in reformed set

parts.note: a black mark is a note against someone's record

indicators.note: the word for always is placed inside the rearranged letters
reformed means remade into a new shape, so the letters of set are rearranged

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, always

explanation.surface: Criminals face disapproval from a reformed crowd who used to be their own set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reformed' gives ETS; 'in' puts the poetic contraction of ever inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Black marketeers trade illegally in scarce goods, so they are lawbreakers.

clue.text: Such deeds must be shocking, if name is tainted

indicators.note: tainted means corrupted or spoiled, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning that scandalous acts ruin a reputation once one's name is sullied.
explanation.definitionFit: Infamous acts are notorious, disgraceful ones, which by their nature shock people.

clue.text: Spider's ending with insect in spout

indicators.note: the ending of the word Spider's is its final letter, taken here

parts.note: an ant is an insect

explanation.surface: A spider finishes off an insect caught in a water spout.
explanation.definitionFit: To spout is to hold forth at length, which is to rave or harangue.

clue.text: Plant in bed we'd zap?

indicators.note: to zap is to blast something, so the letters of the phrase are blown apart and reassembled

explanation.surface: A gardener wonders whether to blast a weed sitting in a bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bindweed is a climbing weed, a convolvulus, found in many gardens.

clue.text: You, on boat's capsizing, may give something less than three cheers

definitions.text: may give something less than three cheers

indicators.note: in a down light the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: ye is the archaic form of you

indicators.note: a capsizing boat turns over, so the word is read upwards in this down light

parts.note: a tub is a slow boat, and tub's (tub has) gives TUBS

explanation.surface: Someone on a capsizing boat is less than wholehearted in cheering.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'yes, but' signals qualified agreement, a reply short of full enthusiasm.

clue.text: The West must take chance with a new leader

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word for chance is replaced by a different one

parts.note: an accident is something that happens by chance

explanation.surface: Western powers are told to gamble under fresh leadership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with a new leader' swaps the A at the front of ACCIDENT for an O.
explanation.definitionFit: The Occident is the western world, the counterpart of the Orient.

clue.text: Deity above celebrated with poems, not half

indicators.note: in a down light the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: something celebrated in song has been sung

indicators.note: not half means half the word for poems is dropped

parts.note: odes are poems

explanation.surface: A god in the heavens is praised in verse, though only partly.
explanation.definitionFit: A sun god, such as Ra or Helios, is a deity of the sun.

clue.text: The wind burns me, a terrible problem for Brits abroad, as before?

definitions.text: problem for Brits abroad, as before?

indicators.note: terrible means dreadful or wild, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Briton abroad complains of windburn, a dreadful problem for travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's poem cast colonial rule as a duty the British had to bear, hence 'as before'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase from Kipling named the supposed duty of colonisers, an imperial burden carried by Britons overseas in the past.

clue.text: With frightful lies around, I mean to get into a row

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the word for mean
frightful means dreadful, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: near is an old word for mean, stingy

explanation.surface: Someone surrounded by dreadful lies means to pick a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frightful' gives LIISE, and 'around' wraps it round the old word for stingy. 'A row' looks like a quarrel but is a line.
explanation.definitionFit: To linearise something is to arrange it in a straight line, a single file.

clue.text: Seat in third row that's painful

parts.note: in a theatre rows are lettered, and the third is row C
ouch is the cry of pain

explanation.surface: A theatregoer finds the seat in row three uncomfortable.
explanation.definitionFit: A couch is a sofa, a seat for several people.

clue.text: A paper held in respect, popularly and skilfully fashioned

indicators.note: the article and paper sit inside the slang word for respect

parts.note: cred, short for credibility, is slang for respect
the FT is the Financial Times, a newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper is held in high regard and its articles are skilfully made.
explanation.definitionFit: Something crafted has been made with skill and care by hand.

clue.text: Woman in high-pressure area within British company

indicators.note: the weather term sits inside the company's initials

parts.note: BT is British Telecom, the UK phone company
a ridge is an elongated region of high pressure on a weather map

explanation.surface: A woman works in a weather system inside a British firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridget is a female first name, so it fits a woman.

clue.text: Funny turns involving one comedy writer

indicators.note: involving means the reversed word wraps around the numeral
turns means the word is read backwards

parts.note: rum means odd or funny-peculiar
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A comic writer's odd routines all involve one person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' makes RUM into MUR, and 'involving' puts I inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Muir was a British comedy writer and broadcaster, known for Take It From Here.

clue.text: PM to conclude with honour? There's a certain lack of belief here

definitions.text: There's a certain lack of belief here

parts.note: Edward Heath was a British prime minister
to end is to conclude
the OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: A prime minister ends his career with an honour, though some doubt it.
explanation.definitionFit: Heathendom is the realm of heathens, those holding no recognised religious faith.

clue.text: One of those bloomers in our beds, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Something growing in our flowerbeds may be a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomers' looks like underwear, but means flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosebud is a rose not yet open, a flower about to bloom.

clue.text: Parent makes request with message, wanting learner to be let off

parts.note: to beg is to make a request

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so a letter is dropped
let off means released, so the letter for learner goes

parts.note: a letter is a written message
L is the learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A parent asks by note for a learner driver to be excused.
explanation.definitionFit: A begetter is one who fathers a child, hence a parent or originator.

clue.text: Agent for change to get a stomach churning over — dope?

indicators.note: churning over means turned around, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: tum is informal for stomach
gen and dope are both slang for information

explanation.surface: Someone takes a drug that leaves their stomach churning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'churning over' turns TUM into MUT; 'dope' looks like a drug but means information.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutagen is a substance or agent that causes genetic mutation.

clue.text: Serving winners against players at the outset? That's ominous

parts.note: men are players, as members of a team, and they come first here
acing is serving aces, unreturnable winners in tennis

explanation.surface: A tennis player serving aces against opponents early on looks threatening.
explanation.definitionFit: Menacing means threatening, which is what an ominous thing seems.

clue.text: Awkward-looking group of people sitting on heather

indicators.note: in a down light the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: a gang is a group of people
ling is a common heather

explanation.surface: An ungainly bunch of people sit on the heather on a moor.
explanation.definitionFit: Gangling describes someone tall, thin and clumsy-looking.

clue.text: Good time to have chaps in field of medicine taking part

indicators.note: the three pieces go inside the medical field's initials

parts.note: ENT is ear, nose and throat, a medical specialty
an age is a period of time
men are chaps

explanation.surface: Men enjoy a good time while working in a medical field.
explanation.definitionFit: Engagement is involvement or participation in an activity.

clue.text: Provided protection for some soldiers

indicators.note: for here means standing in place of the middle, so the soldiers fit inside the word for provided

parts.note: to provide is to give, so gave
the RE are the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: Armour was supplied to a few soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface looks like a statement about supply, but a greave is the protection itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A greave is a piece of armour protecting the shin.

clue.text: Short periods of time for gathering men and children

indicators.note: the abbreviation for minutes gathers in the soldiers

parts.note: mins is short for minutes
OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: There are brief periods for rounding up men and children.
explanation.definitionFit: In law minors are people below the age of majority, so young people.

clue.text: Boss has hit back

indicators.note: back means the word for hit is read in reverse

parts.note: to bonk is to hit

explanation.surface: The boss has struck back.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is a raised knob or stud, as on a shield.

clue.text: Retired tennis player writing about footballers

parts.note: Chris Evert is a retired American tennis champion
on means about, as in a book on a topic

explanation.surface: A former tennis star writes about a football team.
explanation.definitionFit: Everton is an English football club based in Liverpool.

clue.text: More than one such snob offers nonsense

definitions.meaning: snob is an old word for a shoemaker or mender of shoes
'More than one such' makes it plural

explanation.surface: A snooty person keeps talking rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Snob looks like a social climber but is the old word for a shoemaker. Several of them, cobblers, is British rhyming slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoemaker is the old meaning of snob, and the plural form is British slang for rubbish.

clue.text: Fan is foolish old person, no doubt

indicators.note: no means without, so the hesitant sound is removed

parts.note: an old buffer is a foolish old man
er is the sound of hesitation or doubt

explanation.surface: A fan is surely a silly old person.
explanation.definitionFit: A buff is an enthusiast, someone keen on a hobby.

clue.text: English very little used in French street entertainment

indicators.note: the abbreviations are placed inside the French word

parts.note: rue is French for street
V is the short form of very, little signalling the abbreviation

explanation.surface: Hardly any English is spoken in a French street show.
explanation.definitionFit: A revue is a stage show of sketches, songs and dances.

clue.text: Thief with hot goods may do this to keep within bounds

definitions.text: Thief with hot goods may do this
definitions.meaning: a thief may ring a stolen car (give it false identity) and fence the goods (sell them on)
to protect funds by reserving them for one purpose only

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is split: ring and fence are both crimes done with stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring-fence money is to guarantee it is kept for a set purpose and cannot be diverted.
